title: The leg, not the will
hookLine: illness hinders the body, not the will; lameness hinders the leg, not you (Enchiridion 9)
tomorrow: What do I have for this?

cards: A master twists Epictetus' leg. Epictetus says calmly, you'll break it. It breaks.
Didn't I tell you? That's one story of his limp, told by a critic named Celsus and quoted by the Christian writer Origen. The philosopher Simplicius says only that he was lame from his youth.
The ancient sources agree on the limp and disagree about why, and nobody knows which is true. What we do know: the man with the limp is the teacher behind section nine.

teach.h: A HINDRANCE TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.
teach.b: Section nine says illness is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to the will.
The will here is prohairesis, a word Epictetus returns to again and again.
It means the power to choose: to assent or refuse, to judge, to set an aim. For him it's the real self, the part nothing outside can force. Then the habit he asks for.
Say this, he writes, about everything that happens to you, and you'll find it's a hindrance to something else, but not to yourself. The flight is delayed: a hindrance to the schedule.
The voice is gone: a hindrance to the speech. A diagnosis: a hindrance to the body. Each time, a quiet second clause: not to the will.
Now the honest limit. Modern readers sometimes push back here, and fairly. Pain, illness, exhaustion and depression can reach the mind, cloud judgment, make choosing itself hard.
Epictetus isn't pretending a broken leg doesn't hurt. His claim is narrower and stubborn: even inside real limits, something remains to be decided.
How to bear it, what to make of it, who to be while it lasts. Some people living with long illness find that line steadying; others find it too tidy. Both reactions are honest.
And it's worth remembering whose teaching it is: a man who, for one reason or another, spent his life walking on a bad leg.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism, especially while ill or injured, name what a limit actually hinders and remind themselves of what remains theirs to choose.

o: what a limit really hinders, while the will stays free
a symbol of weakness the Stoics tried to hide

games.q: you've lost your voice the morning of a big talk. what does section nine have you say?
o: a hindrance to my voice, not to my will.
games.why: name what it really hinders, then add: not the will. what you do next is still yours.

practice: Notice your body, top to bottom, and find one limit in it: a stiff back, tired eyes, an old injury, a cold.
Name it plainly, this is a hindrance to my back, and then name one thing it can't reach: how you'll speak today, your patience, your attention to this breath. Rest there.

wordCard.voice: The leg. In section nine, the thing a limit actually hinders, the leg, the body, the plan, while the will, the power to choose, stays free. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 9: the will, the power of choice.

carryVoice: Your line: not the will. The limit is real, and so is what's left to choose. That's day three hundred forty-one.
